metadata.title: Associations Between School Climate and Student Mathematics Achievement: A Multilevel Structural Equation Modeling Approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used TIMSS 2019 U.S. eighth-grade data and excluded 10 schools with eight or fewer students to ensure within-cluster variation for multilevel estimation. To account for TIMSS’s complex sampling design, the authors applied both student-level and school-level sampling weights in the multilevel structural equation modeling (MSEM): the total student weight (TOTWGT) for student-level estimates and the school weight (SCHWGT) for school-level estimates. The weights are described as reciprocal selection probabilities with adjustments for nonparticipation, and they are intended to make estimates representative at the corresponding analysis level. The manuscript does not report replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and the analysis instead relies on Mplus maximum-likelihood estimation with robust standard errors (MLR) for inference.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The outcome is TIMSS mathematics achievement measured using five plausible values (BSMMAT01–BSMMAT05). The paper states that these plausible values were used as the mathematics outcome and that standardized scores were calculated, but it does not explicitly describe the statistical combining rule (e.g., Rubin’s rules) or whether analyses were run separately across plausible values and then pooled. Missing data handling is described as full information maximum likelihood (FIML) in Mplus, which is not a standard PV-combining description; therefore, the plausible-values-specific procedure is not fully documented in the text provided.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 U.S. eighth-grade student data. Excluded 10 schools with eight or fewer students because of lack of within-cluster variation for multilevel modeling. Included 235 schools and 7589 students total. No missing values were reported for students’ mathematics scores; missingness for other variables ranged from 2.0% to 4.1% at the student level and 0.9% to 2.3% at the school level, and FIML was used under a missing-at-random assumption.

main_findings.performance_metrics: MSEM fit: CFI=0.964, TLI=0.961, RMSEA=0.018, within-level SRMR=0.055 (between-level SRMR=0.091). Key standardized paths: belonging/safety→achievement b*=0.192 (SE=0.025, p<0.001); math class climate→achievement b*=0.090 (SE=0.037, p=0.014); bullying→achievement b*=-0.087 (SE=0.027, p=0.001); shortage of math resources→achievement b*=-0.320 (SE=0.126, p=0.011); school discipline/safety→achievement b*=-0.183 (SE=0.084, p=0.030). Indirect effects: bullying→belonging/safety→achievement b*=-0.072 (p<0.001); bullying→math class climate→achievement b*=-0.026 (p=0.020).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (U.S.) the study leveraged school belonging and safety, mathematics class climate, bullying, shortage of math resources, and school discipline and safety to model mathematics achievement, finding that belonging/safety and classroom climate were positively associated with achievement while bullying was negatively associated (directly and indirectly). At the school level, shortages of mathematics resources and more discipline/safety problems were negatively associated with achievement. This indicates that strengthening school safety and classroom order, implementing anti-bullying prevention, and improving mathematics instructional resources may be effective levers for raising U.S. eighth-grade mathematics performance, though the cross-sectional mediation framework limits causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzed TIMSS 2019 U.S. eighth-grade data (N=7589 students in 235 schools) to examine how nine school-climate factors at both student and school levels relate to mathematics achievement using multilevel structural equation modeling (MSEM). The mathematics outcome used five TIMSS plausible values (BSMMAT01–BSMMAT05) and the final MSEM showed good fit (CFI=0.964, TLI=0.961, RMSEA=0.018; within-level SRMR=0.055). At the student level, school belonging and safety (b*=0.192, p<0.001) and mathematics class climate (b*=0.090, p=0.014) were positively associated with achievement, while bullying was negatively associated both directly (b*=-0.087, p=0.001) and indirectly via belonging/safety (b*=-0.072, p<0.001) and class climate (b*=-0.026, p=0.020). At the school level, shortages of mathematics resources (b*=-0.320, p=0.011) and school discipline and safety problems (b*=-0.183, p=0.030) were negatively associated, whereas teacher/parent/student characteristics and school support were not significant. Because the design is cross-sectional and mediation is not time-ordered, the results indicate associations rather than causal effects.
